processes.description: Schedulers keep running month-to-date flow spreadsheets for utility and industrial customers such as HL&P, CP&L, Equistar and Mobil, and send updated numbers to the desk as the month goes on. Customers and pipelines send their own actuals or swing volumes back. Differences between Enron's system flow and the customer's meter, short days, plant outages and unrecorded deals are raised by email and resolved before the volumes are agreed for billing.
steps: Pull the latest daily flow for the customer meters from Enron's system or SCADA.
Update the customer's month-to-date spreadsheet and send it to the desk.
Receive the customer's or pipeline's actuals, swing volumes or best-available figures.
Compare the customer's figures with Enron's system flow and flag short days or differences.
Check whether a deal exists for any unexplained gas and whether it was billed.
Adjust nominations or volumes for outages and plant restarts the customer reports.
Agree the final monthly volumes and pass them on for billing.

stalls.summary: A question on whether unbilled CP&L gas actually flowed waited on an answer and was chased on consecutive days by the person handling CP&L.
An HL&P spreadsheet contained errors, so a corrected version had to be prepared and sent again to replace the one already circulated.
SCADA problems interrupted the meter data used for the month-to-date flow update.
Confirmation depends on the counterparty sending its figures first, so the scheduler waits on the customer's email before passing numbers on.

contradictions.summary: Enron's system flow and the customer's own meter figures are kept as separate columns and do not agree, and customers report short days that the desk's numbers must then be reconciled against.
Whether a February CP&L volume was covered by a deal is unclear: one person asks if a deal existed while another says the gas should have been billed on a term deal if one was in place.

automation.approach: A daily report that pulls metered flow from the scheduling system for each customer, lays it beside the customer's or pipeline's actuals in a fixed spreadsheet layout, and highlights days where the two differ or where no matching deal exists, so the scheduler only works the flagged days.
automation.rationale: Most rounds are the same month-to-date spreadsheet rebuilt and resent, and the trouble arises when system flow, customer meters and deals disagree. A standard reconciliation layout with system flow, customer flow, difference and deal columns would make every round consistent and surface mismatches early.

work_estimate.rationale: Each round updates a month-to-date flow spreadsheet from system and meter data, compares it with the customer's figures, and sometimes investigates a short day or missing deal. Routine updates take around a quarter hour; rounds with a discrepancy or deal lookup take longer, giving a mid of 30 minutes. Data pull and comparison are mechanical; judging disputes stays manual.

processes.description: Desk leads and risk staff issue and repeat rules for how deals are booked in Sitara, Enpower, CAPS and EOL: which book or strategy to use, how to enter swaps and storage deals, linking physical deals, documenting changes in comments, and approvals for top-level changes. Rules are often issued after a booking error or mismatch is found, then refined and forwarded again to the traders and schedulers.
steps: Notice a booking problem, mismatch or new business need.
Check the affected deals in the trading system against the intended treatment.
Write or revise the booking rule or procedure, sometimes with an attached document or template.
Get approval where the rule touches protected or top-level items.
Send the rule to the desk and point questions to a named contact.
Follow up on deals that still do not follow the rule and correct them.

stalls.summary: A proposed change went out without replies, leaving the author to ask whether silence meant approval.
A trading limit was broken and the rule had to be restated forcefully, showing earlier reminders had not held.
Deals booked inconsistently or unmatched with external records forced reconciliation work and new booking guidance.

contradictions.summary: The rule that all deals go under ST-Whourly was reissued the next day with exceptions for lending, parking and cuts.
Top-level cells were said to need John Lavorato's approval, yet a later revision unprotected those cells.
Financial deals were earlier booked as annuities, and a later instruction says to stop and use the swap function instead.

automation.approach: Keep one maintained booking procedure per system covering books, strategies, deal types, linking and comment requirements, with a dated change log, and add system checks that flag deals booked to the wrong book or missing a link or change comment.
automation.rationale: The rules are scattered across separate emails and revised piecemeal, so the desk cannot tell which version applies. A single procedure with a change history, backed by simple validation checks, would cut repeated reminders and the reconciliation that follows booking errors.

work_estimate.rationale: Hands-on work is checking the deals behind a problem, matching them against external records, and drafting or revising the rule or attached procedure. Short reminders need little; rounds with a spreadsheet of unmatched deals or a written procedure take longer, so a mid of 25 minutes. Checks can find misbooked deals; writing rules and decisions stay manual.

processes.description: Staff ask report senders to add a group address such as DL-Portland Shift to a distribution, or to correct how a name appears so mail is received. The list owner sometimes asks for the member names, which are then supplied. Requests also gather contact details for new list members.
steps: Notice a missing recipient or a wrong name on a distribution list.
Ask the list owner to add, remove or correct the entry.
Supply the member names or contact details the owner asks for.

stalls.summary: A list owner could not act until given the names of the group's members, because they did not know who does what.
A name change left reports addressed to the old name, so mail was missed until senders updated their lists.

contradictions.summary: One request says the name Bill Williams III must appear for mail to arrive, while a later request asks senders to change it to Bill Williams without the suffix.

automation.approach: Have report senders address shared group lists maintained from the directory rather than personal lists, so name changes and team membership flow through automatically, with a standard request message for adding a list.
automation.rationale: Each round is a short request to add or correct a recipient. A reusable request stating the list, the change and the members removes the back-and-forth over who belongs on the list.

work_estimate.rationale: The hands-on work is editing a list entry or gathering a few member names. The quotes show single additions and name corrections, so a mid of 5 minutes. Directory-driven group lists would handle most edits, leaving confirmations manual.
